beats.act: cold open
beats.narration_text: Ahoj — this is Liam, in for Divyank. The hardest cuts aren't the bad chapters — they're the good ones that just don't serve the reader you signed up for. This chapter is the discipline for deleting on evidence, against a plan, with a reason you can actually defend later.

props.topic: AI1 CLI · CUT TO THE BLUEPRINT
props.command: Explain how to cut a signed book plan's scope down honestly: the evidence a cut needs, the log every exclusion requires, and how to handle a disagreement without letting it drift silently.
output: what you cut is usually fine — that's exactly why it's hard
a cut with no log entry is a disappearance, not a decision
silent drift is the one forbidden move

beats.act: Act I — The Power of No, Made Accountable
beats.narration_text: Cutting is harder than writing, because what you cut is usually fine. It's competent, finished, someone's real work — it just doesn't serve the reader your Blueprint actually named.

beats.act: Act I — The Power of No, Made Accountable
beats.narration_text: The discipline isn't 'delete boldly.' It's delete on evidence, against a plan, with a logged reason — never on a mood. A cut you can't explain later isn't scope control. It's vandalism with a rationalization.

against a signed plan
with a logged reason — never a mood

beats.act: Act I — The Power of No, Made Accountable
beats.narration_text: "Murder your darlings" gets credited to Faulkner, or King. It's actually Arthur Quiller-Couch, in 1916, in a lecture called "On Style." A maxim isn't a method — getting the attribution right is the first sign the method is being taken seriously.

beats.act: Act I — The Power of No, Made Accountable
beats.narration_text: Evidence looks like this: marks on a real page, from a real review — not a feeling about whether a chapter earns its place, but a structural read of whether it serves the reader the plan actually named.

beats.act: Act I — The Power of No, Made Accountable
beats.narration_text: Cut because you're bored of a chapter, and the decision dies with your mood. Cut because the Editorial Review and the signed plan agree it doesn't serve the reader, and the decision survives being questioned later.

beats.act: Act III — Log Every Exclusion, Disagree Once on Purpose
beats.narration_text: Open the drawer, and every record is exactly where it should be — findable, labeled, accounted for. That's the whole purpose of an exclusion log: the difference between a decision and a disappearance.

beats.act: Act III — Log Every Exclusion, Disagree Once on Purpose
beats.narration_text: Every cut gets a record, in four fields: what was cut, why, who decided, and the reopen condition — the circumstance under which it could actually come back.

beats.act: Act III — Log Every Exclusion, Disagree Once on Purpose
beats.narration_text: The real worked example: the memoir and portfolio-reflection chapters weren't cut — they were demoted to a supplemental module, because their relevance depends entirely on who's reading, founder or employed copywriter, not on weak evidence.

beats.act: Act III — Log Every Exclusion, Disagree Once on Purpose
beats.narration_text: Disagree with the plan, and cut it anyway, or silently keep it, and the disagreement just evaporates, unaccountable either way. Resolve it explicitly instead — amend the plan, logged, or make the cut, logged — and the disagreement itself becomes part of the record.

beats.act: Act III — Log Every Exclusion, Disagree Once on Purpose
beats.narration_text: The skill was never obedience to the plan. It's refusing to let a disagreement resolve itself without a trace — one logged disagreement, and its one explicit resolution.

beats.narration_text: A gap this size doesn't fill itself in. Something that was there is now visibly, undeniably missing — and the only way to know what belongs in that space is to have kept the piece, or at least a record of it.

beats.act: Act IV — What Can Go Wrong
beats.narration_text: A chapter just vanished — that means a cut happened with no log entry at all. The fix is to reconstruct the record: what, why, who, reopen. Or the trail stays broken.

beats.act: Act IV — What Can Go Wrong
beats.narration_text: You kept a chapter you were told to cut, and said nothing — that's drift, plain and simple. Resolve it in the open instead: amend the plan, or make the cut. Logged, either way.

beats.act: Act IV — What Can Go Wrong
beats.narration_text: Cut something because the evidence is merely thin, and you've punished uncertainty as if it were a verdict. Name the real reason instead — 'doesn't serve this reader' — and the cut is finally something you can actually defend.

beats.act: Act IV — What Can Go Wrong

beats.act: Act IV — What Can Go Wrong
beats.narration_text: The book is the right size now — everything that doesn't serve the reader is gone, and every absence has a receipt. But what survived was written for a composition course, not a market. Next, the book changes what the survivors actually are.

beats.act: verdict
beats.narration_text: Let's recap with Claude. Cutting is harder than writing because what you cut is usually fine — the discipline is deleting on evidence, against a signed plan, with a logged reason, never on a mood. This book's real cut column: twenty-one chapters convert or merge, two demote to a module, one splits, zero wholly cut — the one global cut was the school apparatus itself, removed everywhere at once. Every exclusion gets a four-field record — what, why, who, and the reopen condition — which is the difference between a decision and a disappearance. And disagreement gets resolved explicitly, never silently: amend the plan, logged, or make the cut, logged — and 'thin evidence' is never a reason by itself. Only 'doesn't serve this reader' is.
